title: Scientific machine learning: PINNs, neural ODEs and neural DAEs

items.context: A PINN's loss has two terms. What does the second one measure?
items.why:
The first term fits the data. The second plugs the network's output and its derivatives
into the equation of motion and squares what is left over, the residual. A function that
obeys the equation exactly makes it zero.
items.true: The residual of the governing equation, zero for a function that obeys it exactly
false: The error against measurements taken after the training window
The size of the network's weights, to keep it from overfitting
The difference between the PINN and a plain network trained on the same data

items.context: Where does the spring-mass PINN evaluate its physics term?
items.why:
The physics term needs no measurements, only the equation, so it can be evaluated
anywhere. Spreading the collocation points over the whole interval is what lets the
equation guide the network after the data run out.
items.true: At 40 collocation points spread over the whole second, including where there is no data
false: Only at the 10 measured time points, where the answer is known
Only after the last measurement, where the data cannot help
At every training step's random batch of measurements

items.context: You raise λ, the weight on the PINN's physics term, and retrain. What happens?
items.why:
The physics is a penalty, so λ sets the exchange rate between the two terms. Making the
residual more expensive shrinks it at some cost in data fit, but a penalty never forces it
to exactly zero.
items.true: The residual shrinks, and the fit to the data gets a little worse
false: The residual becomes exactly zero
Both the residual and the fit to the data improve
Nothing, since λ only rescales the whole loss

items.context:
After training, the PINN's residual is 0.7 N at its 40 collocation points. What is it over
the whole second?
items.why:
The optimizer only sees the residual at the collocation points, so that is where it is
pushed down. Between them nothing penalizes it, and over the whole second the root mean
square is 5.3 N.
items.true: Larger: 5.3 N, because the physics is penalized only where it is evaluated
false: Also about 0.7 N, because the network is smooth between the points
Exactly zero, because the collocation points cover the interval
Smaller, because the residual averages out between the points

items.context:
Both networks fit the 10 spring-mass measurements from the first 0.36 s. After the data run
out, which one is right?
items.why:
With nothing after 0.36 s, the plain network drifts to a flat line (RMSE 0.54 m). The PINN
follows the oscillation (RMSE 0.001 m), because the equation tells it what happens next.
items.true: The PINN; the plain network is wrong by about half a meter
false: Both, since they fit the same 10 points
The plain network, since no residual term compromises its fit
Neither, since no model can say anything past its data

items.context:
The PINN needs the second derivative of the network with respect to time. How does the JAX
code get it?
items.why:
jax.grad returns the derivative of a scalar function. Applied to the network's output as a
function of t, and then again, it gives the exact second derivative. jax.vmap only
evaluates that derivative at many points at once.
items.true: By applying jax.grad twice, differentiating with respect to the input t
false: By finite differences between neighbouring collocation points
With jax.vmap, which returns the derivative at every point at once
With a second network trained to predict the acceleration

items.context:
A recurrent network and a neural ODE are both trained on the same spring-mass data. What
does the neural ODE learn that the recurrent network does not?
items.why:
A recurrent network learns a time-discrete realization of the dynamics, tied to its step
Δt. A neural ODE learns f itself, the arrows on the phase plane, and the solver turns those
into a trajectory at whatever times you ask for.
items.true: The right-hand side f, the vector field, which holds for any starting state and any sampling times
false: The jump from one sample to the next, for one fixed step size
One trajectory x(t), for this release of the mass
The step sizes the ODE solver should take

items.context:
You halve the time step of the recurrent update. What happens to its largest error against
the exact solution of the ODE?
items.why:
Forward Euler's error is proportional to the step size, so halving Δt halves it. On the
spring-mass the largest error went from 0.106 to 0.049 to 0.024 m as Δt halved from
0.0025 s.
items.true: It roughly halves, because forward Euler is first order
false: It drops to about a quarter
It stays the same, because the network has not changed
It doubles, because twice as many steps accumulate error

items.context:
Start from the residual update h_(k+1) = h_k + Δt f(h_k; θ), with f a neural network.
What do you get as Δt goes to zero?
items.why:
Dividing by Δt turns the left side into a difference quotient, which becomes a derivative
in the limit. The recurrent network was a forward Euler discretization of that ODE all
along.
items.true: A neural ODE, dh/dt = f(h, t, θ), of which the recurrent network is the Euler discretization
false: A PINN, because the residual of the update goes to zero
A DAE, because the update becomes an algebraic equation
The same recurrent network, run for more steps

items.context:
In the tank manifold, two tanks must keep equal levels, x0 = x1. Which equation gives the
flow y2 into tank x1?
items.why:
The constraint x0 = x1 holds at every instant, and y2 is the algebraic variable that makes
it hold. No equation states it directly, which is what makes the model a DAE rather than
an ODE.
items.true: None: y2 is whatever keeps the two levels equal
false: A valve equation relating y2 to the pressure drop
The pump equation, since the pump drives every flow
A neural network trained on measured flows

items.context:
A batch reactor's temperature must stay below a limit at every instant. A PINN-style model
puts that limit in its loss as a penalty. Why is that not enough?
items.why:
A penalty trades the constraint against the data fit, so it can leave a small violation,
and it only acts where it is evaluated. A safety limit is a path constraint: it must hold
at every instant, which needs it enforced, not penalized.
items.true: A penalty makes violations small, not zero; the limit has to hold at every instant, as a path constraint
false: A penalty cannot be differentiated, so the optimizer ignores it
Penalties only work for equality constraints
Temperature limits can only be held by a controller, never by a model

items.context: In the simultaneous approach, when are the model equations satisfied?
false: At every iterate, since each iterate is a simulation
Only at the measured time points
Never exactly; they are penalized like a PINN's residual

items.context:
At iteration 0 the simultaneous fit of the spring-mass has a sum of squared errors of 0.00.
Why is it not finished?
items.why:
The states start as an interpolation of the data, so the misfit is zero, but the largest
violation of the collocation equations is 7.7. The solver then repairs the physics, ending
with a defect of 2.5e-15.
items.true: Its states sit on the data but break the model equations
false: It has not computed a gradient yet
The data are noisy, so a perfect fit is suspect
Interior-point solvers always run a fixed number of iterations

items.context:
A team estimates the damping and stiffness of a lightly damped oscillator by single
shooting, starting from k = 150 N/m, and reports μ = 0.29 N·s/m and k = 419 N/m as the
system's values. What did they miss?
items.why:
A simulated oscillation slightly out of phase with the data misfits everywhere, so the loss
has many local minima. The sequential run stopped in one (sum of squared errors 5.23); the
simultaneous run reached the true values within noise (0.036).
items.true: Single shooting can stop in a local minimum on oscillating data; the simultaneous approach from the same start found μ = 0.99, k = 402
false: BFGS needed more iterations to reach the true values
With noisy data, the damping cannot be estimated at all
Single shooting cannot estimate two parameters at once

items.context:
On a new batch, the bioreactor's neural ODE drives the substrate to −0.37 g/L. What does
SiNDAE's neural DAE prediction do differently?
items.why:
In prediction the network equation gets slack variables whose sum is penalized. The solver
keeps the network's growth rate wherever it can, and overrules it only where S would
otherwise go negative.
items.true: Solves the same model as an NLP with S ≥ 0, moving the growth rate off the network's value only where a constraint would break
false: Retrains the network on the new batch before predicting
Clips the substrate at zero after integrating
Integrates with a smaller time step

items.context:
A report says: "The neural DAE never lets the substrate go negative, so it must be more
accurate than the neural ODE on every state." What is wrong with the claim?
items.why:
The constraint stops the prediction from being impossible; it does not make the learned
growth rate correct. On the new batch the neural DAE never goes below zero, yet its
substrate error against the true model (RMSE 0.30 g/L) is larger than the neural ODE's
(0.19 g/L).
items.true: Feasible is not accurate: the neural DAE's substrate error is 0.30 g/L, the neural ODE's 0.19 g/L
false: Nothing: a constraint that holds makes every predicted state more accurate
The neural DAE cannot predict substrate, only biomass
The neural DAE's substrate does go negative, only less than the neural ODE's

items.context:
A projection layer enforces a mass balance A y = b on a network's output. How well does the
output satisfy it?
items.why:
The layer replaces the raw output by the closest point on the constraint, a fixed linear
correction with no trainable weights. Every output it returns satisfies A y = b, whatever
the network upstream does.
items.true: To machine precision, in training and in use
false: Approximately, with the error set by a penalty weight like a PINN's λ
Only on the training data
Only after the network has been trained to convergence

items.context:
A neural DAE and a projection layer both enforce a constraint exactly. Where does each one
do it?
items.why:
A neural DAE writes the constraints into the optimization problem the solver satisfies. A
projection layer is part of the network itself, so every output it returns already obeys
the constraint.
items.true: The neural DAE in the solver; the projection layer in the network, on every forward pass
false: Both in the loss, with a large penalty weight
The neural DAE in the network; the projection layer in the solver
Both after training, by clipping the outputs
